justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from wherever the asset was trading at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 174.5 was anchored closely to the prevailing price, with only a small drift component, since overnight and intraday moves for most liquid assets tend to be modest in percentage terms absent a major catalyst. The one-week estimate of 175.8 reflects a continuation of that gentle positive drift, consistent with a slightly bullish near-term bias — perhaps reflecting positive momentum or a favorable macro backdrop at the time. The one-month estimate of 178.0 extends that trend further but at a diminishing marginal rate, acknowledging that mean-reversion forces and compounding uncertainty make large directional calls less reliable over longer horizons.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, and this is by design. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 13 points (168–181), reflecting normal intraday and overnight volatility. At one week, the interval expands to 26 points (163–189), incorporating the possibility of multi-day trending moves, earnings surprises, or macro data releases. By one month, the interval balloons to 53 points (152–205), capturing the full range of plausible outcomes including sustained trends, reversals, and event-driven shocks. The asymmetry in the intervals — particularly at the monthly horizon — also acknowledges that sharp downside moves can be faster and larger than equivalent upside moves.

Several risks could push outcomes well outside even these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a company-specific shock (earnings miss, legal or regulatory action, executive departure) could drive prices significantly below 152 within a month. On the upside, a blowout earnings report, a major acquisition announcement, or a broad market melt-up fueled by dovish Fed signals could push prices well above 205. These tail events are by definition assigned low probability in the forecast but are not negligible over a one-month window.

It is also worth noting that the stated intervals assume relatively normal market functioning. In periods of acute stress — a credit event, geopolitical escalation, or liquidity crisis — realized volatility can exceed historical norms dramatically, making even wide 90% intervals too narrow. Conversely, if markets enter an unusually calm, low-volatility regime, the actual outcome may cluster far tighter around the point estimate than the intervals suggest. These regime-change risks are the hardest to quantify and represent the most honest source of model uncertainty in any probabilistic price forecast.
